newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lobbies lawmakers to back MFN for China.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lobbies lawmakers to back MFN for China.

text.p: President Clinton met with members of the House of Representatives late on Wednesday and urged them to back renewing most favored nation (MFN) trade status for China, lawmakers said.

Rep. John Porter, an Illinois Republican who has opposed renewing MFN status for China in the past, emerged from the nearly two-hour session at the White House and said he would vote for renewal this time.
Porter said the lawmakers discussed steps that could be taken to foster democracy in China and was satisfied Clinton would support them if MFN status were renewed.

"We discussed these initiatives with the president, principally increasing broadcasts of the Voice of America and Radio Free Asia to China, and increasing the funding for the National Endowment of Democracy's efforts in China," Porter said.
"The president responded very, very positively and we belive we can work with the White House to make these matters real policies for the United States," Porter said.
Rep. David Drier, a California Republican who also said he would vote for MFN renewal, said he found the session with Clinton "to be very positive."

"One of the most interesting things to emerge from our discussions, it seems to me, is the fact that...we want to take a number of steps that will play a role in encouraging political pluralism and democratization ... in China," he said.

Support has been building in Congress to increase radio broadcasts into China and increase funding for the National Endowment, which promotes pro-democracy projects, as an alternative to rejecting MFN.

The influential House Ways and Means Committee voted on Wednesday to back Clinton's decision to maintain normal U.S. trade relations with China. It may be voted on by the full House as early as next week, the lawmakers said.
"The pressure is on for people to vote against it," said Rep. John Murtha, a Democrat from Pennsylvania, who also attended the meeting.

"It's going to be a close vote," he said, noting that he too would support extending MFN. He said he favored diplomatic efforts to win concessions from Beijing, rather than ending current trade relations.
